body:
Regional drainage of Gujarat

Gujarat's rivers can be understood through 3 broad drainage regions: rivers of mainland Gujarat, rivers of Saurashtra and rivers of Kachchh and the northern semi-arid belt.

Many large mainland rivers originate outside Gujarat and enter the state before reaching the Arabian Sea. Saurashtra contains numerous shorter rivers flowing outward from its interior uplands. Northern Gujarat and Kachchh contain seasonal drainage systems associated with the Rann and semi-arid landscapes.

Four major rivers flowing towards the Gulf of Khambhat

RiverSource regionImportant Gujarat location
SabarmatiAravalli Hills, RajasthanGandhinagar, Ahmedabad
MahiVindhyan region, Madhya PradeshMahisagar region
NarmadaAmarkantak, Madhya PradeshEkta Nagar, Bharuch
TapiMultai, Madhya PradeshUkai, Surat

These rivers are encountered broadly in the order Sabarmati, Mahi, Narmada and Tapi when moving from north to south across mainland Gujarat.

Narmada

The Narmada flows westwards across Madhya Pradesh, forms portions of interstate boundaries involving Maharashtra, and enters Gujarat. The Sardar Sarovar Dam is located on the Narmada near Navagam and Ekta Nagar. The river reaches the Gulf of Khambhat near Bharuch.

The Karjan is a tributary of the Narmada in Gujarat. The Karjan Dam is associated with this tributary rather than the main Narmada channel.

Tapi

The Tapi originates near Multai in Betul district of Madhya Pradesh. It flows through Maharashtra before entering Gujarat. The Ukai Dam is situated on the Tapi in southern Gujarat. The river passes through Surat and enters the Arabian Sea near the Hazira region.

Mahi

The Mahi originates in Madhya Pradesh and flows through Rajasthan and Gujarat. Its winding course crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice. Kadana Dam is situated on the Mahi in Gujarat.

Sabarmati

The Sabarmati originates in the Aravalli region of Rajasthan and flows southwards through Gujarat. Gandhinagar and Ahmedabad are associated with the Sabarmati. Dharoi Dam is an important project on the river.

Rivers of northern Gujarat, Saurashtra and southern Gujarat

RiverRegionDrainage association
West BanasNorthern GujaratLittle Rann of Kachchh
SaraswatiNorthern GujaratRann-associated inland drainage
BhadarSaurashtraArabian Sea
ShetrunjiSouthern SaurashtraGulf of Khambhat
MachhuMorbi regionLittle Rann of Kachchh
DamangangaSouthern Gujarat and adjoining areasArabian Sea near Daman

The West Banas of northern Gujarat is distinct from the Banas River of eastern Rajasthan, which belongs to the Chambal-Ganga drainage system.

Southern Gujarat receives relatively high monsoon rainfall compared with Kachchh and northern Gujarat. Rivers in the southern region include the Purna, Ambika, Auranga and Damanganga.

Important dams and river associations

Dam or projectRiverRegion
Sardar SarovarNarmadaEkta Nagar
UkaiTapiTapi district
KadanaMahiMahisagar region
DharoiSabarmatiNorthern Gujarat
DantiwadaWest BanasBanaskantha region
KarjanKarjanLower Narmada basin
MadhubanDamangangaValsad region
ShetrunjiShetrunjiBhavnagar region

A dam stores and regulates river water for purposes such as irrigation, drinking water, electricity generation and flood management. Its name may refer to a nearby settlement rather than the river itself. Correct identification therefore requires remembering both the project and its river.

Prelims focus

  • Sardar Sarovar is on the Narmada.
  • Ukai is on the Tapi.
  • Kadana is on the Mahi.
  • Dharoi is on the Sabarmati.
  • Shetrunji is a river of Saurashtra.
  • Trap: Gujarat's West Banas is not the Banas tributary of the Chambal.

[Sources: GCERT, Class 9, Social Science, Chapter 15, Drainage System, pp. 114–120; NCERT, Class 11, India: Physical Environment, Chapter 3; Government of Gujarat, Narmada, Water Resources, Water Supply and Kalpsar Department, Brief Note on Water Resources Related Issues and Flood Memorandum; Central Electricity Authority, State Profile on Hydro Development for Gujarat, 13 July 2022; Gujarat major dam particulars reported 3 July 2025 by DeshGujarat. Online references consulted 27 November 2026.]
title: Gujarat's Rivers, Dams and Drainage Regions

body:
The western and eastern coasts

India's coastal plains lie between the Peninsular Plateau and the sea. Their width and landforms vary because of differences in the position of mountain ranges, river drainage and the deposition of sediments.

CharacteristicWestern coastal plainEastern coastal plain
Adjacent seaArabian SeaBay of Bengal
General widthRelatively narrowRelatively broad
Adjacent mountain systemWestern GhatsEastern Ghats
Common river-mouth featureEstuariesLarge deltas
Important coastal featuresCreeks, estuaries and backwatersDeltas and coastal lagoons

The western coastal plain is relatively narrow because the Western Ghats lie close to much of the western coastline. Along the eastern coast, major rivers have deposited extensive sediments, producing broad deltaic plains.

Named coastal regions

Coastal regionPrincipal geographical association
Gujarat CoastKachchh, Saurashtra and mainland Gujarat
Konkan CoastMaharashtra and Goa
Kanara CoastKarnataka
Malabar CoastKeralam
Northern CircarsNorthern Andhra Pradesh and adjoining eastern coastal areas
Coromandel CoastTamil Nadu and adjoining southern Andhra Pradesh

Traditional coastal-region names describe physical geographical stretches. Their historical definitions do not always coincide exactly with present state boundaries.

Coastal states and Union Territories

India has 9 coastal states. Along the western coast from north to south are Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka and Keralam. Tamil Nadu extends around the southern end of the peninsula and along the southeastern coast. Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal lie along the eastern coast.

The 4 coastal Union Territories are Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Puducherry, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.

Important gulfs and coastal openings

FeatureGeographical position
Gulf of KachchhBetween Kachchh and Saurashtra
Gulf of KhambhatBetween eastern Saurashtra and mainland Gujarat
Gulf of MannarBetween southeastern India and western Sri Lanka
Palk StraitBetween Tamil Nadu and northern Sri Lanka

A gulf is an extension of the sea into the land. A strait is a relatively narrow water passage connecting larger water bodies and separating land areas.

The Gulf of Kachchh is important for ports, coral ecosystems and marine biodiversity. The Gulf of Khambhat receives the waters of several large Gujarat rivers, including the Narmada, Tapi, Mahi and Sabarmati.

India's revised coastline length

Coastline measurements depend on the scale and resolution at which coastal irregularities are recorded. More detailed measurements capture small curves, creeks and other features that may be omitted in less detailed measurements.

In 2025, the National Hydrographic Office and Survey of India reassessed India's coastline using improved high-resolution data. The revised figures were promulgated through a Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways circular dated 29 April 2025.

RegionOld length (km)Revised length (km)
India, including islands7,516.6011,098.81
Gujarat1,214.702,340.62
Tamil Nadu906.901,068.69
Andhra Pradesh973.701,053.07
Andaman and Nicobar Islands1,962.003,083.50

Under the revised 2025 measurements, Gujarat remains the state with the longest coastline. Tamil Nadu ranks second among states, and Andhra Pradesh ranks third. Andaman and Nicobar Islands has a greater total coastline length than any individual state because it consists of numerous islands.

These are the revised official measurements verified for the 27 November 2026 content cutoff. The reassessment does not mean that the country's land area or physical coastline suddenly increased by a corresponding amount.

Old and revised coastline facts

Older NCERT editions give India's coastline as approximately 7,517 km. The revised official figure is 11,098.81 km. Questions specifying the older textbook measurement and questions asking for the revised official measurement require different answers.

Prelims focus

  • The Konkan Coast is associated with Maharashtra and Goa.
  • The Malabar Coast is associated with Keralam.
  • The Coromandel Coast lies along southeastern India.
  • Gujarat has the longest coastline among Indian states.
  • The revised national coastline length is 11,098.81 km.
  • Trap: Andhra Pradesh ranks third, not second, among states under the revised 2025 coastline measurements.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, 2018–19 edition, Our Country – India, pp. 50–55; NCERT, Class 11, India: Physical Environment, Chapter 2, Structure and Physiography; Ministry of Earth Sciences, Parliament Question: Coastline of the Country, PIB Release 2198800, 4 December 2025, including the revised state-wise table and reference to the circular of 29 April 2025. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
title: Coastal Plains, Gulfs and Revised Coastline Measurements

body:
India's two major island groups

India's principal offshore island groups are the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal region and Lakshadweep in the Arabian Sea. They differ in geological origin, physical appearance and geographical location.

FeatureAndaman and Nicobar IslandsLakshadweep
LocationSoutheast of mainland IndiaSouthwest of mainland India
Marine regionBay of Bengal and adjoining Andaman SeaArabian Sea
Geological characterEmergent submarine mountain system, including volcanic islandsPredominantly coral islands and atolls
CapitalSri Vijaya PuramKavaratti
Important southern islandGreat NicobarMinicoy

The Andaman and Nicobar group forms part of a north-south island chain forming a southward continuation of the Arakan Yoma ranges of Myanmar. Lakshadweep developed primarily through coral growth in warm, shallow marine waters.

Important islands and marine channels

FeatureGeographical relationship
10 Degree ChannelSeparates the Andaman and Nicobar groups
9 Degree ChannelSeparates Minicoy from the main Lakshadweep group
8 Degree ChannelSeparates Minicoy from the Maldives
Barren IslandActive volcanic island in the Andaman region
NarcondamVolcanic island in the Andaman region
Great NicobarContains Indira Point
Pamban IslandRameswaram region of Tamil Nadu
SriharikotaBarrier island of Andhra Pradesh adjoining Pulicat Lake
MajuliRiver island in the Brahmaputra, Assam

A river island develops within a river channel. An oceanic or coastal island is surrounded by marine waters. Majuli is therefore geographically distinct from islands such as Minicoy and Great Nicobar.

Types of lakes

Lakes may develop through river activity, glacial processes, tectonic movements, coastal sediment deposition, volcanic activity, meteorite impact or artificial construction. Their water may be fresh, saline or brackish.

A lagoon is a shallow coastal water body partly separated from the sea by a sand barrier, spit or similar feature. Brackish water has a salt content intermediate between that of typical freshwater and seawater.

Lake or wetlandState or Union TerritoryImportant characteristic
WularJammu and KashmirFreshwater lake associated with Jhelum
DalJammu and KashmirLake in Srinagar
Pangong TsoLadakh and adjoining Tibetan regionHigh-altitude saline to brackish lake
SambharRajasthanInland saline lake
LonarMaharashtraMeteorite-impact crater lake
ChilikaOdishaBrackish coastal lagoon
PulicatAndhra Pradesh and Tamil NaduCoastal lagoon
KolleruAndhra PradeshFreshwater lake between Krishna and Godavari deltas
VembanadKeralamLake and backwater system
LoktakManipurLake containing floating vegetation masses called phumdis
NalsarovarGujaratShallow freshwater wetland

Chilika and Pulicat are associated with coastal processes, whereas Sambhar is an inland saline lake. Lonar is distinct because its origin is associated with a meteorite impact rather than ordinary river deposition.

Backwaters of the southwestern coast

The Malabar coastal region contains lagoons, lakes and interconnected water channels known as backwaters. They form a distinctive landscape supporting fishing, inland transport, agriculture and tourism. Vembanad is an important component of this system.

Gujarat's wetland landscapes

The Great and Little Rann of Kachchh contain extensive seasonal saline landscapes. They become inundated during parts of the rainy season and develop broad salt-covered surfaces during dry periods.

Nalsarovar, Thol and Wadhvana represent inland wetland environments, while Khijadia near Jamnagar contains both freshwater and saline coastal habitats. Chhari Dhand is a seasonal wetland associated with the Banni region of Kachchh.

Prelims focus

  • The 10 Degree Channel separates the Andaman and Nicobar groups.
  • The 9 Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the main Lakshadweep group.
  • Barren Island is volcanic.
  • Chilika is in Odisha; Loktak is in Manipur.
  • Kolleru lies between the Krishna and Godavari deltas.
  • Trap: Sambhar is an inland saline lake, not a coastal lagoon.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, 2018–19 edition, Our Country – India; NCERT, Class 9, Contemporary India-I, Chapter 3, Drainage; NCERT, Class 11, India: Physical Environment, Chapter 2; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, national Ramsar wetland listing reproduced in PIB material dated 6 November 2026; V. N. Kulkarni, Geology of Gujarat, pp. 1–2. Online references consulted 27 November 2026.]
title: Indian Islands, Important Channels, Lakes and Wetlands
